payload.name: Date-specific discussion topic recovery
payload.description: When a question asks what named people discussed or the topic of a conversation on a specific date, use this to require date-aligned evidence and per-participant event searches.
content: When answering what X and Y discussed on a specific date, search each participant's individual events for that date; discussion topics are often stored as separate personal events, not as a joint 'discussion' memory.
Verify that every evidence memory's time range covers the target date; if no date-matching evidence is retrieved, run additional searches with participant names and the date before answering.
Treat 'topic' as possibly multiple topics; combine all date-matching memories rather than stopping at the first candidate.

candidates.solves: The agent failed to retrieve a participant's individual event on the target date because it searched only for a joint 'discussion' memory, then answered using a memory from a different date. The general rule is to treat date-specific discussion questions as requiring time-aligned evidence from each participant's individual events, and to never use non-date-matching evidence. This applies to any question about conversations, meetings, or shared activities on a stated date.

payload.name: Re-search post-event plans with domain terms
payload.description: When a question asks about a subject's plans after a specific event and the first search returns only the event memory, use domain/goal terms and time-bounded retrieval to locate the post-event plan memory.
content: When a question asks what plans or actions a subject has after a specific event (e.g., after advice, a meeting, a networking event), and the first search returns the event memory but no resulting plans, run an additional search using domain/goal terms inferred from the event context and the subject's goals, and restrict the time window to memories with world_start on or after the event date.
Do not answer with older, unrelated plan memories; if the re-search still yields no post-event plan memory, inspect the subject's memories dated from the event onward before finalizing an answer.

candidates.solves: Searches for post-event plans often re-use the event's keywords and miss the plan memory written in different vocabulary. When the first retrieval returns the event but no resulting plans, re-search with domain/goal terms from the event context and constrain world_start to the event date or later. Applies to any 'plans after [event]' question; not to event-description or past-state questions.

payload.name: Retrieve event date for temporal-context questions
payload.description: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with a specific event, retrieve the event and its date first, then infer the season from the date; do not stop after one search that misses the event.
content: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with an event (e.g., wedding, birthday, trip), first retrieve the event memory and its world_start date. Use event synonyms (got married/wedding, was born/birthday) and do not require the holiday or season name to appear in the query or memory text.

If the event memory provides a date but no holiday name, determine the holiday or season from the calendar date (e.g., late December → Christmas season) using general world knowledge, and answer from that date as evidence.

Do not conclude 'No information available' after a single retrieval when the question asks about an event's temporal context; run at least one additional search focused on the event and its date before answering.

candidates.solves: The runtime searched only for combined 'event + holiday' terms and stopped after one retrieval, missing the event memory whose date answers the question. The abstraction: when a question relates any dated event to a holiday or season, first retrieve the event and its date, then infer the period from the date via calendar knowledge. Applies to future questions about weddings, birthdays, trips, graduations, or similar events.

payload.name: Broaden temporal filters for time-qualified retrieval
payload.description: When a question includes a specific time or date and a point-in-time filtered search returns no direct evidence, retry with a broader time range or no time filter before concluding the information is missing.
content: When a user question contains a specific time qualifier (e.g., 'in August 2022'), do not use a point-in-time filter as a hard constraint in the initial search; use a broader time range or omit the time filter, then assess temporal relevance from memory content and timestamps.
If a point-filtered search yields no directly supporting memory, retry the same query with a wider temporal window (or no time constraint) before answering that the information is absent.

candidates.solves: The retrieval failed because a point-in-time filter set to the date in the question (August 2022) excluded a memory whose world_start was later, even though its content directly answered what was shared. This mechanism—over-trusting a question's stated time as a hard retrieval boundary—applies to any time-qualified question, especially when memory timestamps reflect update/recording time rather than event time. A general rule is to broaden or omit temporal filters before declaring an answer absent.

payload.name: Broaden kind and time filters for ongoing activity queries
payload.description: When a question asks what someone read, used, owned, or was engaged in during a time period, search across event, preference, and state memories without strict point-time filtering, because ongoing activities are often recorded as preferences or states.
content: When a query asks about an activity (reading, using, working on, owning) within a time period, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' memories that describe ongoing activities or current status.

Avoid point time_mode filters that exclude records whose world_start is near but after the target period; instead search without a strict time window first, then evaluate temporal relevance from the evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what someone read, used, owned, or was engaged in during a period, restricting retrieval to event memories with strict point-time filtering misses preference/state memories that record ongoing activities with later or loose timestamps. Use this rule for such activity-period questions, not for one-off factual queries where the target event kind and exact date are explicit.

payload.name: Temporal follow-up retrieval for sequence questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone did after, next, or following a described event, and initial results return thematically related events that may not be the actual next action.
content: When a question asks what activity followed an event (after, then, next), first locate the anchor event memory and record its timestamp and source.

Run a follow-up search for the person plus a time window starting at that timestamp, including sequence/action terms such as after, next, visited, and went; inspect memories sharing the anchor timestamp and any co-extracted events from the same source.
Before answering, verify the selected memory describes an action occurring after the anchor event and is not merely a semantically similar event from a different date; otherwise continue searching.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was answering a 'what did X do after Y' question with a thematically related but temporally unrelated memory, because retrieval ranked topic similarity over temporal adjacency. A reusable rule is to resolve sequence queries by anchoring on the prior event's timestamp and preferring memories that share or immediately follow that timestamp. This applies to any future question asking for the next action after a stated event, across all topics.

payload.name: Expand retrieval for shared personal achievements
payload.description: When a question asks what achievement or news one person shared with another, retrieve events about either person alone and use a broader time window instead of requiring both names and exact date.
content: If a query describes an item 'shared with' or 'told to' another person, search for memories whose subject is either person individually; the sharing may be implicit and the memory may mention only the achiever.
Use a broadened time window (e.g., whole stated month or relative phrases like 'last week') rather than a single point date, so recent personal milestones are not excluded.

candidates.solves: Access searches fail when a question pairs two people but the stored event records only one person's achievement or news; requiring both names and an exact point date misses memories with relative timing such as 'last week'. This rule applies to future questions about personal milestones shared between individuals, but not to questions explicitly asking for a joint or collaborative event.

payload.name: Relative-time expansion and evidence time check for temporal questions
payload.description: When a question specifies a time period and memories may store relative dates, expand searches with relative-time variants based on the session timestamp and answer only from memories whose time window overlaps asked period.
content: When a question specifies a time period (e.g., 'second week of November', 'last month'), expand search queries with the relative-time expressions equivalent to that period as measured from the session timestamp (e.g., 'last Friday', 'last week', 'this month'), because memories often store relative dates.

After retrieval, before answering a temporal question, verify each candidate memory's world_start/world_end overlaps the asked time period; discard any candidate whose time window is outside the period even if its semantic or keyword score is high, and continue searching with time-focused variants.

Do not treat memories about future interest, plans, or preferences (e.g., 'expresses interest in visiting X', 'plans to visit X') as evidence of an actual past visit; require a memory that records the event itself within the asked time window.

candidates.solves: Access failed on a temporal question because it never used relative-time variants and accepted a future-interest memory as an actual visit. The rule forces relative-time query variants from the session timestamp and requires evidence to overlap the asked period and record an actual event, not interest or plans; applies to where/when/what questions about a specified period with relative-dated memories.

payload.name: Avoid anchoring on first topic when retrieving specific events
payload.description: Use when a question about a specific past event (what someone shared/made/photographed/posted in a period) yields only partial topical matches; apply before answering to diversify queries and require direct evidence.
content: When a question asks about a specific past event (e.g., what someone shared, made, photographed, or posted in a given period) and no retrieved memory explicitly asserts the full claim (subject + object + time), do not answer from the closest topical matches.

Run at least one additional search before answering, varying the content terms: combine the subject and time window with synonyms/terms from the event's activity and likely outcome domain instead of repeating the topic that dominated the first results.
For such event questions, memories about plans, habits, preferences, or recurring topics are circumstantial; answer only when a retrieved memory directly asserts the event's object.

candidates.solves: Questions about a specific past event (what someone shared/made/photographed/posted in a period) fail when the agent anchors on a recurring topic from the first retrieval, narrows later searches to it, and answers from plan/habit memories. The rule—diversify with the event's activity/outcome terms and require direct event-specific evidence—transfers to any multi-topic subject and time-bounded event question.

payload.name: Temporal-anchor post-milestone retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did or planned after a dated milestone event (e.g., after a wedding) and the first search results appear unrelated or pre-date the event.
content: When a question asks what someone did or plans to do after a dated milestone event, use the milestone date as a temporal anchor; run searches with typical follow-up activity terms (honeymoon, celebration, get-together, trip, activity) and filter or rank memories with world_start on or after that date.
If the first retrieval returns only memories dated before the milestone, do not answer from them; re-search with additional related terms and compare time windows.
Treat pre-milestone memories as non-evidence for post-milestone questions even when they share location or activity vocabulary.

candidates.solves: Post-milestone questions fail when retrieval matches the milestone vocabulary (wedding, bride) and returns older, superficially similar memories while the true post-event activities use different terms (honeymoon, get-together) and later dates. Anchoring on the milestone date, expanding with sequel-activity vocabulary, and discarding pre-milestone memories fixes this mechanism. This applies to any 'after [event]' question about a person's activities or plans; it does not apply when the needed information predates the milestone or no milestone date is available.

payload.name: OrdinalEventDateRetrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for the date of an ordinal occurrence (e.g., third win, first visit), search broadly for base-event memories and use world_start timestamps, including relative-time references, to infer the date.
content: When a question asks when an ordinal event (second, third, nth) happened, do not search only with the ordinal and explicit date words; issue additional searches using the base event without the ordinal (e.g., 'tournament win' if asked 'third tourney win').

Treat memory world_start as date evidence even if the text expresses time relatively ('last week', 'yesterday'); use the session or message timestamp to resolve the relative reference into a concrete date before deciding.

Before answering an ordinal-date question, collect all candidate event memories from multiple searches, sort them by world_start, and identify the requested ordinal by chronological order; do not assume the only explicitly dated memory is the requested ordinal.

candidates.solves: When answering when an ordinal event (e.g., third win) occurred, retrieval often misses memories whose text uses relative time ('last week') and whose date is only in world_start; the agent then mistakes another explicitly dated event for the requested ordinal. Fix: search base event without the ordinal, treat world_start as concrete date, and order candidates chronologically to select the requested ordinal. Not applicable when a single explicit dated memory directly answers a non-ordinal question.

payload.name: Date-bounded event retrieval with count verification
payload.description: When a question asks for events within a specific date range or month, use explicit temporal filters and verify all expected events are retrieved before answering, including follow-up synonym searches when the count seems incomplete.
content: If the question specifies a date range or month, use structured or hybrid search with world_start/world_end filters covering that whole range instead of relying only on natural-language temporal phrases in the query.

Before answering a count question, verify the retrieved evidence satisfies the requested count; if not, issue additional searches using synonyms for likely milestone event types such as marriage, birth, pregnancy, move, or job change.
Do not treat a later announcement or related mention as evidence that the underlying event occurred in the target period; check the event's world_start date.

candidates.solves: Solves incomplete retrieval for questions that specify a date range or month: the system must apply explicit temporal filters and continue searching until the stated number of events is supported by evidence with world_start in the range. It does not apply to open-ended questions without temporal constraints or to construction-side memory updates.

payload.name: Time-bound retrieval for date-specific questions
payload.description: When the question contains an explicit time window (e.g., month/year), use it as a retrieval filter and only accept evidence whose recorded time falls inside that window.
content: If the question names a specific month or year, run a structured search with a temporal filter: include memories whose world_start is on or before the window end and whose world_end is null or on or after the window start.
Before using a retrieved memory as evidence, check its world_start/world_end against the question window; reject memories outside the window even if they are semantically similar.
If the first results all fall outside the window, continue searching with time-constrained queries instead of answering from the closest later memory.

candidates.solves: When a user asks about an activity, event, or state that began within a specific month or year, the agent may retrieve later semantically similar memories and answer with a different item from outside the requested timeframe. The failure mechanism is ignoring explicit temporal scope during retrieval and evidence selection. This skill applies to any time-bounded factual question over memory, not to general open-ended questions.

payload.name: Search plan memories for future attendance questions
payload.description: When a user asks when someone is attending, going to, or planning a future event, include plan memories in retrieval and expand around intention verbs.
content: When a question asks about a future or scheduled activity (e.g., 'when is X attending...', 'when will X go to...'), run retrieval with memory_kind including both 'plan' and 'event' since future intentions may be stored as plan memories with world_start dates.
If the initial results contain no direct date, re-query with expansions such as 'plans to attend', 'will attend', 'scheduled to attend', 'next month/week' and do not restrict to event kind.
Use the world_start of a retrieved plan memory as the temporal anchor for answering 'when' questions.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because retrieval filtered to event memories only, missing a plan memory that recorded a future conference date. Temporal 'when' questions about upcoming activities require searching plan memories alongside events, since plan memories carry world_start dates. This applies to any future question asking when an entity will attend, visit, or participate in something.

payload.name: Time-bounded plural recall search
payload.description: When a question asks for all items within a specific time period, use a time-filtered structured search and verify completeness before answering.
content: If the question contains a time constraint (e.g., a month/year or date range), issue a structured search that filters memories by world_start/world_end falling within that period; relevant memories may use relative time and lack literal date words.

When the question uses a plural target noun (e.g., places, events, people), treat the answer as potentially multi-valued; after the first search, judge whether the evidence set is complete and run additional searches (e.g., broader keywords or time-range filter) before answering.
Resolve relative time expressions in memories (e.g., 'last month', 'last week') against the message/session timestamp to decide if they fall inside the requested period.

candidates.solves: This addresses incomplete retrieval when answering time-bounded recall questions that expect multiple items. The diagnosed cause was that a memory mentioning a target location was missed because it used a relative time expression and lacked literal date keywords, while the search relied only on keyword/semantic expansion. The abstraction is a decision rule to use structured time-range filters and completeness checks, applicable to any future question with an explicit time window and a plural recall target.

payload.name: Date-specific retrieval follow-up
payload.description: When a query asks about an event on a specific date and the first memory search returns no event on that date, run an additional search using the date and subject before answering no information.
content: If a user question contains a concrete date and a subject (person/entity), and your initial retrieval returned no memory whose world_start matches that date, perform at least one additional search that combines the subject with the date as a keyword or structured filter before answering 'no information'.
Do not rely only on semantic similarity for date-specific questions; use date-filtered or keyword retrieval to catch events whose phrasing differs from the query.

candidates.solves: When a date-specific question retrieves no memory for that date, the agent often gives up after one hybrid search, even though an event memory with the exact date exists but ranked below the cutoff. Perform at least one additional date-and-subject filtered or keyword search before concluding no information; this applies to any future 'what happened on [date] for [person/entity]' query.

payload.name: Time-range search for period questions
payload.description: When a user asks about activities/classes/events that happened or started in a period (e.g., mid-August, during June), search with a time_range covering the full period and query expansions for started/enrolled/joined.
content: For questions that name a time period (e.g., mid-August 2023, early June, during 2023), use a time_range spanning the full period instead of a single point-in-time target, so events whose start date falls later in the period are still retrieved.
Expand searches for enrollment/activity questions with verbs like started, began, joined, enrolled, took, and include event/state memory kinds to match memories phrased as 'started taking X classes'.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what events, classes, or activities occurred or started within a named period (e.g., 'mid-August', 'last week'), a point-in-time search at the period's midpoint can exclude later-starting events, causing missed answers. Use a full-period time_range and expand verbs like started/enrolled/joined; do not apply this when the question specifies an exact calendar date/time point.

payload.name: Temporal consistency check before answering
payload.description: When a question specifies a time period for an event, verify each retrieved memory's world_start/world_end overlaps the period before using it as evidence; re-search with time filters if top candidates are temporally inconsistent.
content: When the question specifies a time window, before answering check every candidate memory's world_start/world_end and discard any whose range does not overlap the window, even if the text seems semantically relevant.

If no valid evidence remains, re-search with a structured time filter (e.g., world_start within the window) and broaden activity verbs (trip, visit, retreat, vacation) instead of repeating only the exact wording from the question.
Never answer using a memory whose date contradicts the question's timeframe unless another retrieved memory explicitly places the event inside the window.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was answering a time-bounded question with a semantically similar memory whose date was outside the window. The reusable fix is to check each candidate's world_start/world_end against the question's period before answering, and re-search with time-filtered queries plus broader activity terms when candidates are temporally invalid. Applies to any future question that anchors an event to a date range.

payload.name: Verify explicit event timing evidence
payload.description: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started), require evidence that explicitly states that event's timing; do not substitute a related event's date (publication, exhibit, announcement).
content: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started, created), verify the cited memory explicitly describes that event and its timing. Do not answer with the date of a related event (publication, exhibition, announcement) unless a memory explicitly equates that date with the requested event's time.

If retrieved memories only concern related events or lack explicit timing for the requested event, judge the evidence insufficient and run additional searches using temporal/completion phrases (e.g., 'completed', 'finished', 'a few days ago', 'recently') and structured filters on the relevant subject/predicate (e.g., artwork/created/completed).

When a search returns a memory with explicit relative timing (e.g., 'a few days ago'), resolve the date from the memory/session timestamp and cite that memory as evidence rather than the related-event memory.

candidates.solves: Questions asking when a specific event happened (completion, finish, start) fail when the agent uses a related event's date (publication, exhibition, announcement) or answers without explicit timing evidence. The rule requires explicit temporal evidence for the requested event and adds completion-focused supplementary searches, applying to any 'when did X finish/complete Y' question across topics.

content: If the question specifies a date range or month, use structured or hybrid search with world_start/world_end filters covering that whole range instead of relying only on natural-language temporal phrases in the query.

Before answering a count question, verify the retrieved evidence satisfies the requested count; if not, issue additional searches using synonyms for likely milestone event types such as marriage, birth, pregnancy, move, or job change.
Do not treat a later announcement or related mention as evidence that the underlying event occurred in the target period; check the event's world_start date.
operations.reason: Creating merged Skill for date-range count retrieval.

operations.name: Search plan memories for future attendance questions
operations.description: When a user asks when someone is attending, going to, or planning a future event, include plan memories in retrieval and expand around intention verbs.
content: When a question asks about a future or scheduled activity (e.g., 'when is X attending...', 'when will X go to...'), run retrieval with memory_kind including both 'plan' and 'event' since future intentions may be stored as plan memories with world_start dates.
If the initial results contain no direct date, re-query with expansions such as 'plans to attend', 'will attend', 'scheduled to attend', 'next month/week' and do not restrict to event kind.
Use the world_start of a retrieved plan memory as the temporal anchor for answering 'when' questions.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for future plan retrieval.

operations.name: Date-specific retrieval follow-up
operations.description: When a query asks about an event on a specific date and the first memory search returns no event on that date, run an additional search using the date and subject before answering no information.
content: If a user question contains a concrete date and a subject (person/entity), and your initial retrieval returned no memory whose world_start matches that date, perform at least one additional search that combines the subject with the date as a keyword or structured filter before answering 'no information'.
Do not rely only on semantic similarity for date-specific questions; use date-filtered or keyword retrieval to catch events whose phrasing differs from the query.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for date-specific follow-up.

operations.name: Verify explicit event timing evidence
operations.description: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started), require evidence that explicitly states that event's timing; do not substitute a related event's date (publication, exhibit, announcement).
content: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started, created), verify the cited memory explicitly describes that event and its timing. Do not answer with the date of a related event (publication, exhibition, announcement) unless a memory explicitly equates that date with the requested event's time.

If retrieved memories only concern related events or lack explicit timing for the requested event, judge the evidence insufficient and run additional searches using temporal/completion phrases (e.g., 'completed', 'finished', 'a few days ago', 'recently') and structured filters on the relevant subject/predicate (e.g., artwork/created/completed).

When a search returns a memory with explicit relative timing (e.g., 'a few days ago'), resolve the date from the memory/session timestamp and cite that memory as evidence rather than the related-event memory.
operations.reason: Creating new Skill for explicit timing evidence.
